report.label: Required to report
report.explain: A reporting standard (PRISMA-ScR / PRISMA 2020 / PRISMA-S) requires you to REPORT this. It does not always require you to DO it — but if you don't, you must say so.

guidance.label: Methodological guidance
guidance.explain: Recommended by established methodological guidance (JBI, Cochrane, Arksey & O'Malley, Levac et al.). Widely accepted; deviate only with a reason.

convention.label: Convention — varies
convention.explain: Common practice, but no agreed rule. Fields and supervisors differ. Choose, state your choice and why.

tool.label: Choice of this tool
tool.explain: How this tool happens to do it. Not a scientific requirement; other tools do it differently.

Scoping review.definition: A review that maps the concepts, evidence types and gaps in a field, rather than answering a narrow effectiveness question. Usually no pooling of results and often no quality appraisal.

Systematic review.definition: A review that answers a focused question with an explicit, reproducible method, including appraisal of the included studies.

PRISMA-ScR.definition: The 22-item reporting checklist for scoping reviews. It tells you what to report, not how to conduct the review.

PCC.definition: Population – Concept – Context: the JBI framework for formulating scoping-review questions and eligibility criteria (the scoping counterpart of PICO).

Protocol.definition: The plan of the review written before searching: questions, criteria, sources, search, selection, charting and synthesis. Changes after it is fixed are reported as amendments.

Registration.definition: Publicly time-stamping the protocol (e.g. on OSF), so readers can compare plan and report. PROSPERO does not accept scoping reviews.

Amendment.definition: A documented change to the protocol after it was fixed, with date and reason.

Concept block.definition: A group of synonyms for one concept, joined with OR; blocks are joined with AND.

Boolean operators.definition: AND (all concepts must occur), OR (any synonym may occur), NOT (exclude records with a term — risky, it also removes relevant records that mention it).

Truncation / wildcard.definition: A symbol (usually *) that matches any word ending: repairab* finds repairable, repairability. Syntax differs between databases.

Field tags.definition: Where in the record a term is searched, e.g. Scopus TITLE-ABS-KEY (title, abstract, keywords), Web of Science TS (topic).

Test set / relative recall.definition: Papers known in advance to be relevant. The share of them that a search retrieves (relative recall) estimates how complete the search is.

Precision.definition: The share of retrieved records that are relevant. In reviews, precision is often low (a few percent) because completeness has priority.

Deduplication.definition: Removing records that appear in more than one database or version. Usually by DOI, then by title/author/year.

Title/abstract screening.definition: First selection stage: deciding on the basis of title and abstract only.

Full-text screening.definition: Second stage: reading the full report and applying the criteria; exclusion reasons are reported.

Cohen's kappa (κ).definition: Agreement between two raters corrected for agreement expected by chance. 1 = perfect, 0 = chance level.

Snowballing.definition: Finding studies through the references (backward) and citations (forward) of included studies, in iterations until no new studies are found.

Grey literature.definition: Material not published in journals: reports, standards, theses, policy documents.

Data charting.definition: Scoping-review term for data extraction: recording predefined items from each included source in a charting form.

Critical appraisal.definition: Assessing the methodological quality / risk of bias of each included study.

PRISMA flow diagram.definition: Diagram of the number of records identified, screened, excluded (with reasons) and included.

OpenAlex.definition: A free, open index of scholarly works used here for pilot counts, snowballing and open-access links.

idea.what: Dated notes on what you want to find out and why.
how: Write a note whenever your view changes.
Vague is fine; stage 1 makes it precise.
rules: The question may be refined as you read.
Scoping review = map a field; systematic review = answer a focused question.

questions.what: Turn the idea into review questions using Population – Concept – Context.
how: Say why you changed a version.

concepts.what: Split the question into concepts; list every synonym per concept.
how: Add spellings and neighbouring terms; * for word endings.
rules: Synonyms with OR, concepts with AND.
Avoid NOT: it also removes relevant records.
Have the strategy checked by a librarian (PRESS).

queries.what: The concept table translated into each database's syntax.
how: Copy each string into the advanced search.
Edit by hand only if needed.
rules: Report the full search for ≥ 1 database (PRISMA-ScR 8); PRISMA-S: all.
Not Google Scholar as main source: not reproducible.

pilot.what: Test the string: manageable hits, and does it find papers you already know?
how: Look at what was missed and why.
rules: Check the search against known papers.

protocol.what: The plan of the review, written before searching.
rules: Say whether a protocol exists and where (PRISMA-ScR 5).

registration.what: Freeze the protocol; later changes become logged amendments.
rules: Report registration, or that there was none (PRISMA-ScR 5).
Registering scoping reviews: encouraged, not required.

searches.what: Import every final export with exact string, date and filters.
how: Paste the string exactly as run.
rules: Report sources, coverage and date last searched (PRISMA-ScR 7).
Report records per source and limits (PRISMA-S).
Remove duplicates and report how many.
Dedup by DOI, then title/year — check by hand.

screening.what: Apply the criteria: title/abstract first, then full text.
rules: Report the selection process and exclusions (PRISMA-ScR 9, 14).

reviewer.what: A second person screens a random sample blind; agreement as Cohen's κ.
how: An AI may fill the sheet (AI assistance card), but report it as an AI, not a second person.
rules: Report how many screened and whether independently (PRISMA 2020 item 8).
Two independent screeners, ideally for all records.
κ ≥ 0.6 as 'good enough' — the bands are arbitrary.
Counting an AI as the second reviewer — no agreed rule yet; say so and name the model.

snowballing.what: Search the references and citations of included studies.
how: Seeds = studies included at full text.
New records go back through 8 · Screening and 10 · Retrieval (same criteria).
Stop when a round adds no new included study.

retrieval.what: Get the full text of everything that passed title/abstract.
how: Open access first, then your library.
rules: Report reports sought and not retrieved (PRISMA 2020 flow).

charting.what: Record the same data items from every included source.
rules: Report the charting process and items (PRISMA-ScR 10–11).
Pilot the form; ideally a second person checks.

appraisal.what: Rate the quality of each included source.
how: Pick a tool that fits the designs (e.g. MMAT).
rules: Usually not required in scoping reviews.
Some argue it should be considered.

report.what: Flow diagram, checklist and exports for writing.
how: Numbers in the text = PRISMA flow.
rules: Report numbers per stage, ideally as a flow diagram (PRISMA-ScR 14).

items: Repair scores (French index, EN 45554) are spreading. How do researchers measure how repairable a phone or laptop is — and do the methods agree?
Assessment of repairability / ease of disassembly
Which methods are used to assess the repairability of consumer electronic products, and how are they validated?
Which indicators? · Which products? · How was validity tested?
repairab* · reparab* · ease of repair · disassembl*
smartphone* · mobile phone* · laptop* · tablet* · consumer electronic*
concepts.lesson: 'disassembl*' catches ease-of-disassembly methods that never say 'repair'.

queries.code: TITLE-ABS-KEY((repairab* OR reparab* OR "ease of repair" OR disassembl*) AND (smartphone* OR "mobile phone*" OR laptop* OR tablet* OR "consumer electronic*") AND (assess* OR scor* OR indicator* OR index OR metric*))
queries.lesson: OpenAlex has no wildcards: repairab* becomes 'repairability' there.

pilot.lesson: 4× more hits for one extra paper. The missed papers point to a too-narrow product block (add 'electrical and electronic equipment') — and one test-set paper was out of scope.

items: Include: methods that assess repairability of consumer electronics. Exclude: repair-behaviour studies without a method; non-electronic products.
